SK2221 The [UnsafeAccessor] names a member its target does not have

An [UnsafeAccessor] declaration names a member the target type does not declare, or names a field where the target has a method, so the runtime binds nothing and the first call throws.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severityerror
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

UnsafeAccessorAttribute is bound by the runtime, not by the compiler. The member name is a string, nothing checks it, and a typo compiles cleanly and then throws the first time the accessor is called — usually in production, because the accessor is on a path the tests do not take. It is a compile-time-knowable fact reported at run time, which is the trade an analyzer exists to undo.

⚠ Every shape this rule reports was confirmed by running it, not by reading the documentation. On .NET 10, a name the target does not declare throws MissingFieldException — Field not found: 'Target._buffer'; a Field kind naming a member that is a method throws the same; and UnsafeAccessorKind.Constructor with Name = "Create" throws `BadImageFormatException`, "Invalid usage of UnsafeAccessorAttribute", which is harsher still. The correctly spelled field accessor and the unnamed constructor accessor both succeeded in the same run, so the probe was measuring the rule's subject rather than a broken harness. That is what justifies error severity.

Example

Instead of:

[UnsafeAccessor(UnsafeAccessorKind.Field, Name = "_buffer")]
static extern ref byte[] Buffer(Target target);   // the field is called `buffer`

Write:

[UnsafeAccessor(UnsafeAccessorKind.Field, Name = "buffer")]
static extern ref byte[] Buffer(Target target);

When it does not fire

⚠ The target type must be declared in this compilation's own source, and that restriction is the whole reason the rule can be trusted. A reference assembly does not carry private members — stripping them is what a reference assembly is for — so GetMembers("secret") against a type from a referenced assembly returns nothing whether the member is genuinely absent or merely not published. Reporting on that would turn every correct cross-assembly accessor, which is the commonest use of the attribute by a wide margin, into a false error at error severity. The rule reports what it can prove: for a target the compilation itself declares, the member list is complete and a missing name is missing. The cost is stated plainly rather than hidden — the cross-assembly case, which is most of the attribute's use, is not covered by this rule at all.

⚠ Signature comparison is not attempted, and the omission is deliberate. Overload resolution against a private member set, through ref, in, out, generic substitution and the attribute's own convention that the first parameter is the receiver, is a second implementation of the runtime's binder — and a binder that is subtly wrong reports working code as broken. What is checked instead is the fact that needs no binder: whether any member of the named kind answers to that name at all. Base types are walked, because the runtime looks up the hierarchy and a rule that stopped at the declared type would report an inherited private helper as absent.

⚠ Generic accessors are not reported, though an upstream idea proposes it: generic [UnsafeAccessor] support was added after the attribute shipped, the set of shapes the runtime accepts is version-dependent, and the analyzer cannot tell which runtime the assembly will load on. An accessor on a generic type is skipped for the same reason.

⚠ A member that was accessible all along is not reported either. Reaching a public field through [UnsafeAccessor] is pointless rather than broken, and the two are different findings with different severities; this rule is only about the declaration that throws.

`UnsafeAccessorKind.Constructor` is checked without any member lookup, so that one part does hold cross-assembly: the runtime looks for .ctor and nothing else, and a Name set to anything else names something that will never be found. The whole analyzer withdraws when System.Runtime.CompilerServices.UnsafeAccessorAttribute does not resolve.

⚠ No fix. The repair is the member's real name, and the rule knows only that the written one is wrong. Guessing from a near match would be inventing a binding, which is the thing this rule exists to stop.
